title: Good schools first
author: Carousel
summary: Carousel uses a thought experiment — twin brothers Johnny and Jamie placed in two schools on the same street — to argue that school quality, particularly the behavioural and pedagogical environment, explains more of student outcomes than any individual programme or specialist intervention. School A is well-run with consistent expectations, routinised classrooms, and strong pedagogy; School B is not. The article traces how the same student has dramatically different educational trajectories depending on which school they attend, and uses Progress 8 data to illustrate the scale of the school-quality effect. The essay argues that reformers too often target interventions at individual students without first asking whether the school environment makes those interventions viable. It concludes that the priority must be creating genuinely good schools before overlaying more sophisticated or expensive programmes.
points: The most powerful variable in student outcomes is not the programme applied to the individual student but the quality of the school environment they inhabit.
School A and School B on the same street, serving the same community, produce radically different outcomes — because of the school, not the students.
Progress 8 data consistently shows that school quality explains a larger share of variance in outcomes than any specialist programme or targeted intervention.
Reformers who target interventions at individual students without first asking whether the school environment makes those interventions viable are pointing solutions at the wrong level.
Good schools must come first — specialist overlays and intervention programmes work only when laid on top of a fundamentally functional school environment.
quotes: And, if they did, we would then be more comfortable separating the Simons from the Johnnys and saying “yes, this child is better suited to an alternative route aged 14.” But, critically, until a school is performing well, that option will remain a sticking plaster masking a deeper problem.

And when we look at schools which have fixed those problems, we see students who are able to make choices from a more level playing field and a position where they can really evaluate the available options and which one works best for them.

Further down the line, he finds staying motivated during his GCSEs hard, but keeps his head up and leaves school with a string of grade 5s and 6s, including English, maths, science, history, Spanish, RE and design and technology.

But the story represents a truth that lies at the heart of our school system, which is that some schools are better than others, meaning that the same student at different schools will have varying experiences.

Once a student is in a good school with strong behaviour, routinised classrooms, high participation and strategic approaches to long-term memory then we can find establish if they genuinely don’t fit that mold.
Before we start labelling students or moving them onto different curricular pathways, we need to make sure that we’ve done everything else first: if the school isn’t good, we need to start there.
GCSE season comes around, and while Jamie manages to make it into school for all his exams, he often gives up halfway through the paper and doesn’t attend any additional revision sessions.
